back: The loss of water vapour from leaves: water evaporates from mesophyll cell surfaces into the air spaces, then diffuses out through the stomata.
Moves water and mineral ions up the xylem; cools the leaves by evaporation; supplies water for photosynthesis and keeps cells turgid.
Evaporation from the leaves draws water out of the xylem, pulling up a continuous column of water held together by attraction between water molecules.

front: Factors that increase the rate of transpiration
back: Higher temperature, higher wind speed, higher light intensity, larger leaf area and LOWER humidity.

front: Why does high humidity slow transpiration?
back: There is more water vapour in the air, so the concentration gradient from the leaf to the air is smaller and diffusion is slower.

front: What does a potometer measure, and how?
back: The rate of water uptake by a leafy shoot, by timing an air bubble moving along a capillary tube (rate = distance ÷ time).
notes: Uptake is slightly more than transpiration, because some water is used in photosynthesis and for turgor.

front: Volume of water taken up in a potometer capillary
back: $V = \pi r^2 l$, where $r$ is the radius of the capillary and $l$ is the distance the bubble moves.

front: Why is a potometer shoot cut and fitted under water?
back: To stop air entering the xylem, where a bubble would block the continuous column of water.
It loses water faster than it absorbs it, so its cells lose water by osmosis, become flaccid and can no longer hold up the leaves and soft stems.

front: Petroleum jelly experiment: which leaf loses least water (apart from one coated on both surfaces)?
back: The leaf with jelly on its lower surface, because most stomata are in the lower epidermis.

front: Leaf features that reduce water loss (ZIMSEC)
back: Thick waxy cuticle; fewer stomata; sunken stomata; hairs; rolled leaves; small leaves or spines; shedding leaves in the dry season.
